question_text: How are prosthetic groups different from co-factors?

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.50, printed question 155. insider_note: A prosthetic group IS a kind of cofactor, so the honest answer is that one is a subset of the other. Say that and the comparison makes sense.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Prosthetic groups
steps.margin_note: Organic, tightly bound, one example. Three lines.
lines: Prosthetic groups are ORGANIC compounds that
are TIGHTLY bound to the apoenzyme.
Example: the haem group of peroxidase.
steps.why: Prosthetic groups are one of the three kinds of cofactor, so their definition is narrower than the general term and adds the words 'organic' and 'tightly'.
common_mistakes: Saying prosthetic groups are inorganic. They are ORGANIC.
Calling them loosely bound. Tightly bound is the defining feature.

steps.label: Co-factors
steps.margin_note: Define the wider term, then list the three kinds. The subset point is the mark.

lines.text: Every prosthetic group is a cofactor; not
every cofactor is a prosthetic group

lines: A cofactor is the whole NON-PROTEIN part of a
holoenzyme, bound to the enzyme to make it
steps.why: The general term covers three kinds, and prosthetic groups are only one of them — which is the actual difference the question is asking about.
common_mistakes: Treating the two as unrelated. A prosthetic group IS a cofactor, of one particular kind.
Saying cofactors are always organic. Metal ions are inorganic cofactors.
steps.memory_tip: Cofactor is the family; prosthetic group is one member of it.
